title: Base de Datos Anatómica Completa para Aplicación Fitness

b425a764-9fd0-4bbd-aed1-4e91ec8256f9.content:
Estoy haciendo una web app fitness, esta busca relacionar todos los musculos con toda la base de datos de ejercicios que se ha recopilado (mas de 1500 ejercicios) con ficha técnica, video de demostración, musculos de fuerza usados, estabilizadores, movilidad requerida, sustituciones.
Se tiene una base de datos de musculos pero es muy superficial, se tiene las categorías principales:
Abdominal Group
Core
Adductor Group
Legs
Ankle & Foot Stabilizers
Legs
Biceps Group
Arms
Calf Group (Triceps Surae)
Legs
Deltoid Group
Shoulders
Erector Spinae
Back
Forearm Group
Arms
Gluteal Region
Legs
Hamstring Group
Legs
Hip Flexor Group
Core
Latissimus Dorsi & Teres Major
Back
Pectoral Region
Chest
Quadriceps Femoris
Legs
Rotator Cuff Group
Shoulders
Scapular & Thoracic Muscles
Thorax
Trapezius & Rhomboids
Back
Triceps Brachii Group
Arms
Y cada categoría contiene un par de musculos contenidos dentro. 
Lo que quiero es que sea 100% preciso y completo, se debe incluir todos los musculos del cuerpo. Lo ideal es tener ayudas audiovisuales, si encuentras en la web algun modelo muscular gratuito para uso medico o cientifico o academico sería ideal tener acceso a él, ya sea 3d o 2d.
No quiero que la base de datos se quede en los musculos, la app busca integrar salud articular, tratamientos para tendinitis, por lo tanto también tendones y nervios. Así que es importante realizar una investigación completa para recolectar toda la información pertinente cientifica y academica anatomica: sistema muscular, de tendones, de nervios que se pueden lesionar por ejercicios fisicos y de articulaciones.
La idea es poder relacionarlos entre sí con literatura academica de estos temas y que se pueda ver la ficha completa de cada uno de estos musculos, tendones, nervios y articulaciones.
La info que si o si debe haber es: Nombre, nobre cientifico, grupo muscular al que pertenece, extremidad a la que pertenece, origen, incerción, función, rol biomecanico, aesthetics, (en caso de musculos) ejercicios que trabajen dicho musculo, (en caso de articulaciones, nervios o tendones) ejercicios para sanar lesiones del mismo y ejercicios que pueden ponerlo en riesgo.
Necesito que generes los json correspondientes y ojala estén relacionados con algun artefacto, app, asset, recurso cientifico / academico disponible

I am curating an accurate and detailed inventory of human musculature, ensuring every muscle is documented with its origin, insertion, action, and functional role.  
I am integrating related connective tissues such as tendons and ligaments, mapping their anatomical relationships to muscles and joints.  
I am also incorporating neural pathways and joint structures to provide a holistic view of movement mechanics, supporting precise exercise design and injury prevention.

I am systematically cataloging key muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints involved in physical activity, focusing on their biological and mechanical roles.  
For each structure, I am identifying its name, scientific designation, anatomical location, origin and insertion points, primary functions, biomechanical contributions, aesthetic significance, and relevant training or rehabilitation protocols.  
I am also integrating verified academic sources to ensure accuracy and accessibility of information.

I am evaluating publicly available datasets and digital repositories that offer detailed, accurate representations of human musculature.  
This includes assessing structural completeness, resolution quality, licensing compatibility, and integration potential with scientific workflows.  
Based on this evaluation, I will compile a structured JSON output reflecting the most viable and comprehensive anatomical resources.

I am designing a scalable JSON schema that interconnects muscles, tendons, nerves, joints, and exercises through unique identifiers.  
I am curating a substantial yet manageable sample dataset focusing on major anatomical entities relevant to exercise science.  
I am also identifying authoritative open-access resources where the full anatomical database can be programmatically retrieved.

I am systematically organizing foundational human anatomy data, focusing on major muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints relevant to fitness and movement science.  
I am verifying and compiling a curated list of authoritative, freely accessible scientific resources, including open-source 3D models, anatomical databases, and educational platforms, ensuring each is properly attributed and legally usable.  
My aim is to deliver a reliable, up-to-date, and ethically sourced reference that supports both learning and practical application in health and fitness domains.

I am synthesizing a curated collection of authoritative, openly accessible anatomical models and data, prioritizing scientific accuracy and usability.  
These include high-resolution 3D organ and musculoskeletal structures from trusted institutions like NIH, DBCLS, and Harvard-affiliated projects, all under permissive licenses.  
I am also integrating structured ontologies and practical tools to support research, education, and clinical applications across disciplines.

I am identifying reliable, openly licensed anatomical resources to ensure accuracy and compliance, prioritizing those with permissive licenses suitable for data extraction.  
I am organizing the information into a coherent schema that captures muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints with detailed attributes such as origin, insertion, function, and innervation.  
This structured approach enables the creation of a robust, reusable JSON dataset aligned with academic standards and open-access principles.

I am focusing on assembling a high-quality, curated subset of major muscles with detailed functional data, supported by reliable sources.  
I am leveraging open-access anatomical resources that provide structured data through standardized ontologies and downloadable models.  
These foundations enable scalable, accurate expansion of the dataset programmatically while ensuring scientific integrity.

Estoy consolidando fuentes confiables y abiertas, combinando la exhaustividad de Uberon y FMA con información funcional de OpenStax y Physiopedia, complementada con modelos 3D accesibles bajo licencias libres.  
El diseño del modelo se basa en identificadores únicos y relaciones claras entre estructuras anatómicas, asegurando interoperabilidad y rastreabilidad mediante referencias externas como FMA, Uberon y Wikidata.  
Finalmente, estoy estructurando los datos en formato JSON con un esquema coherente que facilita su uso en aplicaciones científicas, educativas o de simulación.

I am curating a meticulously structured overview of all major skeletal muscles, prioritizing accuracy and coverage while balancing practicality.  
I focus on delivering detailed profiles for the most essential muscles, supported by a compact taxonomy that includes all names and identifiers.  
The framework enables seamless expansion into full anatomical data through trusted external sources.

I am identifying reliable public resources, including anatomical databases and structured Wikipedia content, to ensure accuracy and completeness.  
I’m constructing a well-organized JSON structure that captures essential anatomical details—origin, insertion, function, associated exercises—while maintaining consistency across entries.  
The final deliverables include a core set of key muscles, a full index for reference, and dedicated tendon data, all designed for practical use in education and application development.

I am prioritizing clarity and conciseness by focusing on a curated set of representative muscle cards, reducing redundancy while preserving essential anatomical information.  
I aim to maintain comprehensive coverage through a streamlined index that captures key attributes for each structure without overwhelming the output.  
This approach ensures the response remains within practical limits while delivering meaningful, accessible insights.

I am synthesizing data from authoritative public repositories to compile accurate, standardized muscle anatomy entries.  
Each entry includes origin, insertion, and function, aligned with established anatomical nomenclature.  
The resulting dataset serves as a reliable seed for building a dynamic anatomical database.

I am constructing detailed descriptions of muscles, tendons, and nerves with accurate origins, insertions, functions, and innervations.  
I am ensuring clinical relevance by including pathologies and functional contexts such as epicondylitis or nerve entrapments.  
I am maintaining clarity and elegance while avoiding technical jargon overload or reference to tools or processes.

I am systematically organizing musculoskeletal anatomy into functional groups, aligning nerves, joints, and muscles with targeted rehab exercises and contraindicated movements.  
I ensure comprehensive coverage by integrating deep stabilizers like the pelvic floor, diaphragm, and intrinsic hand and foot muscles, while preserving the user’s original 18 groupings and filling in essential gaps.  
This structured approach enables precise, clinically relevant guidance tailored to both therapeutic intervention and risk mitigation.

I am mapping muscle groups to a regional taxonomy while preserving the user's existing categorizations and enriching them with precise anatomical relationships.  
I am verifying each term against authoritative sources to ensure accuracy and consistency with international standards.  
I am integrating structured data from reliable ontologies to enhance the depth and scientific validity of the classification.

I am identifying reliable, freely accessible sources for 3D models, anatomical nomenclature, and structured muscle data.  
My focus is on verifying licensing terms, especially CC-BY compliance, and locating machine-readable formats like JSON or CSV.  
I am compiling authoritative references that support accurate, reproducible anatomical mapping for research or educational use.

I am ensuring accuracy by avoiding speculative assignments of identifier values, recognizing the risks of introducing errors.  
Instead, I am relying on established ontologies and databases to validate relationships and attributes.  
The approach prioritizes integrity over immediacy, aligning with best practices in biomedical data curation.

I am cross-referencing anatomical terminology and identifiers to ensure accuracy, focusing on established databases like FMA and TA2.  
I consider the hierarchical relationships within anatomical classifications, particularly for skeletal muscles in humans.  
My goal is to provide reliable information by relying on trusted resources rather than assumptions.

I am identifying open-access, high-quality 3D muscle models suitable for medical, scientific, and academic use, prioritizing those with permissive licensing and direct downloadability.  
I evaluate each resource based on its availability, compliance with open science principles, and relevance to the user’s need for educational or research applications.  
My focus is on balancing accuracy, usability, and freedom from restrictive copyright barriers.

I am systematically evaluating publicly available anatomical datasets and visual materials to identify reliable, legally compliant sources for educational and research use.  
My focus includes 2D illustrations from Wikimedia Commons, such as public domain plates from Gray’s Anatomy and CC-BY-SA vector graphics, as well as structured data from Terminologia Anatomica and Wikidata.  
I am also verifying the availability of 3D models, including those from NIH’s 3D Print Exchange and BodyParts3D, ensuring their licensing permits reuse and redistribution.

I am assessing a curated set of open-access anatomical datasets, each offering distinct advantages in format, licensing, and utility. The collection spans interactive web platforms, mobile applications, and specialized software integrations, ensuring broad compatibility across research and educational contexts. These resources collectively support detailed 3D visualization, accurate anatomical referencing, and flexible deployment in both academic and commercial environments.

Estoy construyendo una arquitectura basada en entidades musculares y sus relaciones funcionales, asegurando que cada componente esté respaldado por fuentes científicas verificadas.  
Aprovecho recursos de alta calidad como atlas anatómicos históricos, bases de datos de ejercicios y contenidos educativos abiertos, integrándolos bajo licencias compatibles para uso académico y práctico.  
Extiendo la taxonomía original a un sistema más completo y detallado, garantizando cobertura exhaustiva de los grupos musculares del cuerpo humano.

I am structuring the entire muscular anatomy by grouping over two hundred named muscles according to functional and anatomical coherence, ensuring each category reflects both clinical relevance and biomechanical logic.  
I am meticulously aligning scientific nomenclature with common terms while preserving bilateral symmetry and hierarchical clarity across all groups.  
This foundational taxonomy enables efficient downstream mapping of tendons, nerves, joints, and exercises, maintaining balance between depth and manageability.

I am systematically evaluating the coverage of major muscle groups in the body, ensuring no significant components are overlooked.  
I recognize that critical areas such as neck muscles, respiratory and pelvic floor structures, intrinsic hand and foot muscles, and deep stabilizers remain unaccounted for.  
My focus is on achieving comprehensive anatomical representation by identifying and integrating these essential yet often neglected regions.

I am curating a comprehensive, compact inventory of skeletal muscles grouped by anatomical function and location, ensuring each entry includes precise scientific nomenclature.  
I am designing a flexible cross-referencing system that aligns with established anatomical standards like TA2 and FMA, enabling seamless integration with digital anatomy platforms without relying on unverified identifiers.  
My focus is on clarity, accuracy, and interoperability, allowing future linkage to 3D models and digital resources through standardized naming conventions.

I am cross-referencing Wikidata's classification of human muscles with established anatomical ontologies like FMA, TA98, and Uberon to ensure accuracy.  
I am assessing whether Wikipedia’s list of skeletal muscles provides a trustworthy, comprehensive crosswalk between muscle names and their corresponding anatomical identifiers.  
My goal is to deliver a precise, reusable SPARQL query grounded in verified data.

I am verifying the presence of standardized nomenclature codes and structural groupings within the target table to ensure accuracy and consistency.  
Based on this validation, I am curating a representative subset of detailed muscle profiles that reflect all major anatomical categories while maintaining brevity and clarity.  
The selected entries exemplify a uniform schema applicable to every muscle in the complete index, ensuring completeness without exceeding practical limits.

I am curating a comprehensive yet practical list of human muscles grouped by anatomical function, focusing on axial and limb musculature essential for movement and fitness applications.  
I am ensuring completeness by including all major muscles relevant to physical performance while acknowledging the existence of facial expression muscles as part of broader anatomical knowledge, though excluding them from training focus.  
My approach balances anatomical rigor with usability, aligning with the intent of a fitness-oriented resource without compromising accuracy.

I am structuring skeletal muscles into clinically relevant, physiologically integrated groups based on their roles in movement, stability, and regional function.

The useful information in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_skeletal_muscles_of_the_human_body for user goal Confirm whether the muscle tables include identifier columns (FMA, TA98/TA2, Wikidata) and list the main muscle group sections covered as follows: Evidence in page: ## Table explanation and summary [edit] The muscles are described using anatomical terminology. The columns are as follows: | Name | Explanation | | --- | --- | | Muscle | US English[a] name of the muscle per Terminologia Anatomica (TA),[13] minus the term "muscle", with the words reordered occasionally for better sorting. Parts and bellies are listed out as separate rows, as they are sometimes considered separate muscles. - Anything denoting the muscles relationship to another muscle such as e.g. superior, inferior etc. should always be used as a suffix and not a prefix, to create better sortability of the list. | | Location | The location of the muscle in a standard human body. The location first specifies a group such as head, neck, torso, upper limbs, or lower limbs, then may have more specific information. However this additional information must be describing location not function. | | Origin | The bone or other structure the muscle is attached to that remains immobile during the action. The term "bone" is omitted from bone names. | | Insertion | The attachment point of the muscle, on a bone or otherwise, that moves during the action. | | Artery | The artery which supplies the muscle with blood. The term "artery" is included to avoid confusing columns. | | Nerve | The nerve(s) which tell the muscle to act (innervates the muscle). The term "nerve" is included for clarity. | | Action | The movement performed by the muscle from the standard anatomical position. In other positions, other actions may be performed. | | Antagonist | The muscle which can 'cancel' or to some degree reverse the action of the muscle. Muscle synergies are noted in parentheses when relevant. | | O (Occurrences) | Number of times that the named muscle row occurs in a standard human body. Here it may also be denoted when a given muscles only occurs in a male or a female body. By (F) for female and (M) for male, if nothing is denoted. The muscle can be assumed to occur in both genders. This gender denomination should always be behind the number, not in front of it. | | TA | The number of rows in the table for the relevant Terminologia Anatomica muscle. For example, TA splits the nasalis muscle into transverse and alar parts, so their TA column entries are 2. | ### Summary in numbers [edit] There does not appear to be a definitive source counting all skeletal muscles. Different sources group muscles differently, regarding physical features as different parts of a single muscle or as several muscles. There are also vestigial muscles that are present in some people but absent in others, such as the palmaris longus muscle.[14][15][16] There are between 600 and 840 muscles within the typical human body, depending on how they are counted.[17][18][19] In the present table, using statistical counts of the instances of each muscle, and ignoring gender-specific muscles, there are 753 skeletal muscles. ## 7️⃣ Pipeline para completar el 100% de fichas (automatizable)

1. **Nomenclatura + IDs canónicos**: consulta Wikidata por estructura con `P1402` (FMA), `P1323` (TA98) y `P7173` (TA2) [[115]][[118]][[121]]; valida nombre científico contra TA2Viewer [[116]].
2. **Origen/inserción/inervación/acción/antagonista**: scrapea la tabla de *List of skeletal muscles of the human body* (CC BY-SA), que ya trae esas columnas para ~289 filas/753 músculos [[extractor]]; complementa con OpenStax (CC BY 4.0) [[26]].
3. **Asset 3D por músculo**: usa el FMA ID obtenido para enlazar la pieza correspondiente en BodyParts3D [[14]] o buscarla en Z-Anatomy (CC BY-SA 4.0) [[5]].
4. **Ejercicios por músculo**: cruza tu BD de 1500 ejercicios contra el directorio músculo→ejercicio de ExRx [[79]].
5. **Rehab/lesiones**: enlaza artículos de Physiopedia (CC BY-SA) por entidad para los campos de rehab y riesgo [[89]].
6. **Imágenes 2D**: láminas de Gray's (dominio público) por nombre latino [[64]].

Ejemplo SPARQL (Wikidata, CC0) para el crosswalk:
```sparql
SELECT ?item ?lat ?fma ?ta2 WHERE {
  ?item wdt:P1402 ?fma.
  OPTIONAL { ?item wdt:P7173 ?ta2. }
  ?item rdfs:label ?lat. FILTER(LANG(?lat)="la")
} LIMIT 1000
```

Con esto tu app queda **100% trazable a estándares académicos** (TA2/FMA), con assets 3D/2D legales y relaciones músculo↔tendón↔nervio↔articulación↔ejercicio listas para consumir. ¿Quieres que en el siguiente paso genere las fichas detalladas del resto de músculos por lotes (p. ej., antebrazo + mano, o pierna completa)?

The useful information in https://docs.google.com/document/d/14DvWi5OtE8AToSQU0dFUIQCA11MlX0JIY01XEjVIldo/edit?usp=sharing for user goal Extract the audit findings, problems identified, and missing information mentioned in the document as follows: 

Evidence in page: 
## 1. RESUMEN EJECUTIVO DE LA AUDITORÍA

La arquitectura del proyecto que presentas es sólida y técnicamente acertada para una aplicación web moderna y de alto rendimiento. Elegir 2D SVG interactivo como capa base en combinación con Deep-linking / visores 3D (Z-Anatomy y BodyParts3D) resuelve de forma elegante los problemas de rendimiento en móviles, la falta de estandarización de nombres de malla en modelos 3D y las restricciones de licencias libres (CC BY-SA).

Sin embargo, tras analizar el código ejecutable y las bases de datos JSON, se identificaron omitidos clave en la cobertura anatómica, fallos de ejecución e inconsistencias en JavaScript/SVG y simplificaciones biomecánicas que comprometen la precisión científica requerida para una app de fitness y rehabilitación.

## 2. AUDITORÍA DE COBERTURA ANATÓMICA

### 2.1. Sistema Muscular (Evaluación de 147 Entidades / 27 Grupos)

- Estado Actual: El JSON 01_grupos_musculares.json lista 147 músculos/grupos clasificados en 27 categorías. No obstante, en 02_musculos_fichas.json solo existen 32 fichas detalladas (un 22% del total). El resto (115 músculos) recurren a un mensaje "stub-note" sin datos de origen, inserción o biomecánica.
- Agrupaciones Problemáticas para Fitness/Rehab:
    1. Cuádriceps (MUS-110): En las fichas se agrupó como una sola entidad. En entrenamiento y patología femoropatelar es crítico diferenciar el Vasto Medial Oblicuo (VMO) (alineación patelar), Vasto Lateral y Recto Femoral (único biarticular, no se estimula eficientemente en sentadillas debido a la Paradoja de Lombard).
    2. Isquiosurales (MUS-115): Agrupar Bíceps Femoral, Semitendinoso y Semimembranoso oculta que la Cabeza Corta del Bíceps Femoral es monoarticular (solo flexiona rodilla, no actúa en Peso Muerto Rumano/RDL) y que el desgarro en sprint ocurre predominantemente en la cabeza larga del bíceps femoral.
    3. Deltoides (MUS-063..065): Deben mantenerse como 3 haces independientes con diferentes planos de alineación de fibras respecto al plano escapular.
- Músculos Omisos Importantes:
    - Infraespinoso y Redondo Menor (manguito rotador posterior, imprescindibles en la desaceleración de lanzamientos y salud glenohumeral).
    - Poplíteo (el "desbloqueador" articular de la rodilla; clave en tendinitis poplítea).
    - Serrato Posterior Superior e Inferior (mecánica respiratoria y dolor torácico).
    - Tensor de la Fascia Lata (TFL) (síndrome de la centella o fricción de la banda iliotibial).
    - Coracobraquial (estabilidad anterior del hombro).
    - Pronador Cuadrado y Supinador Corto (estabilidad distal de antebrazo y codo).

### 2.2. Sistema Tendinoso (15 Tendones Registrados)

- Brechas Clínicas y de Entrenamiento:
    1. Falta de distinción entre Tendón Patelar y Tendón del Cuádriceps: Aunque ambos pertenecen al aparato extensor de la rodilla, la tendinopatía patelar ("rodilla del saltador") se trata con sentadilla declinada/Spanish squat, mientras que la del cuádriceps afecta la inserción superior de la rótula en levantadores pesados.
- Omisiones Fundamentales:
    - Tendón de la Pata de Ganso (Pes Anserinus): Inserción común de Semitendinoso, Grácil y Sartorio en tibia medial. Una de las bursitis/tendinitis más comunes en corredores.
    - Tendón del Psoas-Ilíaco: Causa principal del "resalte de cadera" (snapping hip syndrome).
    - Tendón Distal del Tríceps Braquial: Tendinopatía insertiva en olécranon muy común en press banca pesado y fondos.
    - Tendón del Pectoral Mayor (Inserción Humeral): Sitio crítico de desgarro en levantadores de potencia.
    - Tendones Abductor Largo y Extensor Corto del Pulgar: Responsables de la Tenosinovitis de De Quervain (frecuente por agarres y en CrossFit).

### 2.3. Sistema Nervioso (14 Nervios Registrados)

- Brechas Clínicas y Atrapamientos de Ejercicio:
    1. Nervio Interóseo Posterior (PIN - Ramo Profundo del Radial): Pasa por la arcada de Frohse en el supinador. Se confunde frecuentemente con codo de tenista (epicondilitis lateral) refractario a tratamiento.
    2. Nervio Obturador: Entrapamiento en el canal obturador, causa común de dolor inguinal crónico e inexplicable en atletas.
    3. Nervios Glúteos Superior e Inferior: Responsables de la inervación de glúteo medio y mayor; su inhibición o atrapamiento en el espacio subglúteo causa "amnesia glútea".
    4. Nervio Musculocutáneo: Inerva bíceps y braquial; vulnerable en tracciones violentas o hipertrofia del coracobraquial.
    5. Nervio Toracodorsal y Pectorales: Involucrados en el Síndrome del Desfiladero Torácico (TOS).

### 2.4. Sistema Articular (13 Articulaciones Registradas)

- Brechas Articulares:
    1. Articulación Esternoclavicular (SC): La única unión ósea real del miembro superior con el esqueleto axial. Fundamental para el ritmo escapulohumeral completo (>90° de elevación).
    2. Articulación Femoropatelar: Debe analizarse como entidad funcional separada de la femorotibial. El Síndrome de Dolor Femoropatelar (SDFP) es la consulta #1 por dolor de rodilla en gimnasios.
    3. Articulaciones Radioulnar Proximal y Distal (PRUJ / DRUJ): Gobiernan la pronosupinación del antebrazo; fallas aquí generan dolor en codo o muñeca durante culls con barra recta.
    4. Articulación Tibiofibular Superior: Causa de dolor lateral de rodilla en sentadilla profunda con rotación externa excesiva.

## 3. AUDITORÍA TÉCNICA Y ERRORES DE CÓDIGO DETECTADOS

During execution testing, the following technical bugs and integration issues were discovered:

| ID Bug | Componente | Error Detectado | Impacto | Solución Aplicada |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BUG-01 | renderFicha (JS) | Mapeo de propiedad inconsistente: el JSON usa e.musculo o e.mus, y algunos valores contienen rangos como "MUS-071..074". | Crasheaba el listener onclick o intentaba buscar el ID literal "MUS-071..074" en la BD, devolviendo undefined. | Se implementó un parser de rangos y unificación de propiedades (e.musculo || e.mus). |
| BUG-02 | SVG Highlight | Al seleccionar ejercicios como Curl de Bíceps (EX-06), el JS intenta iluminar MUS-067 (Braquial). Sin embargo, MUS-067 no existía como elemento <path> en el SVG. | Falla silenciosa: la interfaz listaba el músculo en texto pero el atlas no resaltaba ninguna zona visual. | Se dibujaron los trazados SVG para músculos profundos y se agregó lógica fallback para indicar la región si el SVG es omitido. |
| BUG-03 | viewOf Dictionary | El diccionario viewOf registraba la primera vista donde aparecía un ID. Si una articulación o nervio (ej. ART-001, NER-008) existía en ambas vistas, al buscarlo desde la vista posterior forzaba un cambio brusco a la vista anterior. | Mala UX en navegación y parpadeo de interfaz. | Se preserva la vista actual si la entidad está disponible en ambas ilustraciones SVG. |
| BUG-04 | Formato de Tooltip | El tooltip posicionado con e.clientX / e.clientY sufría desbordamiento (overflow) cerca de los bordes derecho e inferior de la pantalla en dispositivos con pantallas <1200px. | El texto del tooltip se cortaba fuera del viewport. | Se agregaron cláusulas de contención de bordes (Math.min con ancho de pantalla). |
| BUG-05 | Búsqueda por texto | La búsqueda no limpiaba los resaltados previos de ejercicios al hacer clic en un resultado de texto. | Confusión visual entre el ejercicio activo y el músculo individual seleccionado. | Se ejecuta clearSel() y reseteo de clases de ejercicio antes de renderizar la nueva selección. |

## 4. CORRECCIONES BIOMECÁNICAS Y APLICACIÓN AL ENTRENAMIENTO

Para elevar la calidad del atlas a un nivel académico y profesional de fitness, se han corregido los siguientes principios biomecánicos dentro del dataset de fichas:

1. Paradoja de Lombard y Selección de Ejercicios:
- Problema previo: Asignar la sentadilla como ejercicio estrella del cuádriceps sin especificar qué cabezas se estimulan.
- Corrección: La sentadilla genera contracción simultánea de cadera y rodilla; el Recto Femoral apenas cambia de longitud. Se indica explícitamente que para hipertrofiar/rehabilitar el Recto Femoral se requieren Extensiones de Rodilla o Sissy Squat, mientras que los Vastos dominan en la sentadilla.
2. Reclutamiento Diferencial de Isquiosurales:
- Problema previo: Asignar el Peso Muerto Rumano (RDL) para todo el grupo de isquiosurales.
- Corrección: El RDL estimula fuertemente las cabezas biarticulares (Semitendinoso, Semimembranoso, Bíceps Femoral Cabeza Larga). La Cabeza Corta del Bíceps Femoral únicamente se recluta en ejercicios de flexión de rodilla (Leg Curls).
3. Mecánica del Triceps Surae (Gastrocnemio vs. Sóleo):
- Problema previo: Elevación de talones genérica.
- Corrección: Con la rodilla extendida (de pie), el Gastrocnemio (biarticular) asume la mayor parte de la tensión. Con la rodilla flexionada a 90° (elevación de talón sentado), el Gastrocnemio se acorta activamente y el Sóleo asume más del 80% de la carga.

Summary: 
The audit identified several critical issues compromising the project's scientific accuracy and completeness. Key problems include significant gaps in anatomical coverage, where only 22% of muscles have detailed data, with the rest being placeholders. Major biomechanical simplifications were found, such as treating multi-part muscle groups (e.g., quadriceps, isquiosurales) as single entities, which is incorrect for training and rehab. The system also omits important structures like the popliteus muscle and key tendons like Pes Anserinus. Technically, there are bugs causing crashes and visual failures due to inconsistent property mapping and missing SVG paths for deep muscles. Furthermore, the document highlights a lack of distinction between clinically relevant but similar structures, such as the patellar and quadriceps tendons.

Identifying gaps and inconsistencies across anatomical systems and digital interface elements

I am addressing gaps in muscle detail by distinguishing individual components such as the VMO, vastus lateralis, and rectus femoris within the quadriceps, and separating the short head of the biceps femoris from the hamstrings due to its distinct biomechanics.  
I am integrating missing muscles including the infraspinatus, teres minor, popliteus, serratus posterior, TFL, coracobrachialis, pronator quadratus, and supinator to ensure full anatomical coverage.  
Additionally, I am adding the previously omitted tendons—Pes Anserinus and Psoas-Iliacus—as well as their distal connections to complete the structural integrity of the system.

I am assessing structural omissions in musculoskeletal and nervous system components, noting absent tendons, nerves, and joints that compromise anatomical completeness  
Simultaneously, I am evaluating technical flaws affecting data consistency, visual rendering, and user interaction, particularly around property mapping, hidden muscle visibility, and responsive design challenges  
These observations guide a holistic refinement of both content accuracy and interactive functionality to ensure seamless, precise anatomical representation

messages.content:
Estoy haciendo una web app fitness, esta busca relacionar todos los musculos con toda la base de datos de ejercicios que se ha recopilado (mas de 1500 ejercicios) con ficha técnica, video de demostración, musculos de fuerza usados, estabilizadores, movilidad requerida, sustituciones.
Se tiene una base de datos de musculos pero es muy superficial, se tiene las categorías principales:
Abdominal Group
Core
Adductor Group
Legs
Ankle & Foot Stabilizers
Legs
Biceps Group
Arms
Calf Group (Triceps Surae)
Legs
Deltoid Group
Shoulders
Erector Spinae
Back
Forearm Group
Arms
Gluteal Region
Legs
Hamstring Group
Legs
Hip Flexor Group
Core
Latissimus Dorsi & Teres Major
Back
Pectoral Region
Chest
Quadriceps Femoris
Legs
Rotator Cuff Group
Shoulders
Scapular & Thoracic Muscles
Thorax
Trapezius & Rhomboids
Back
Triceps Brachii Group
Arms
Y cada categoría contiene un par de musculos contenidos dentro. 
Lo que quiero es que sea 100% preciso y completo, se debe incluir todos los musculos del cuerpo. Lo ideal es tener ayudas audiovisuales, si encuentras en la web algun modelo muscular gratuito para uso medico o cientifico o academico sería ideal tener acceso a él, ya sea 3d o 2d.
No quiero que la base de datos se quede en los musculos, la app busca integrar salud articular, tratamientos para tendinitis, por lo tanto también tendones y nervios. Así que es importante realizar una investigación completa para recolectar toda la información pertinente cientifica y academica anatomica: sistema muscular, de tendones, de nervios que se pueden lesionar por ejercicios fisicos y de articulaciones.
La idea es poder relacionarlos entre sí con literatura academica de estos temas y que se pueda ver la ficha completa de cada uno de estos musculos, tendones, nervios y articulaciones.
La info que si o si debe haber es: Nombre, nobre cientifico, grupo muscular al que pertenece, extremidad a la que pertenece, origen, incerción, función, rol biomecanico, aesthetics, (en caso de musculos) ejercicios que trabajen dicho musculo, (en caso de articulaciones, nervios o tendones) ejercicios para sanar lesiones del mismo y ejercicios que pueden ponerlo en riesgo.
Necesito que generes los json correspondientes y ojala estén relacionados con algun artefacto, app, asset, recurso cientifico / academico disponible

I am curating an accurate and detailed inventory of human musculature, ensuring every muscle is documented with its origin, insertion, action, and functional role.  
I am integrating related connective tissues such as tendons and ligaments, mapping their anatomical relationships to muscles and joints.  
I am also incorporating neural pathways and joint structures to provide a holistic view of movement mechanics, supporting precise exercise design and injury prevention.

I am systematically cataloging key muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints involved in physical activity, focusing on their biological and mechanical roles.  
For each structure, I am identifying its name, scientific designation, anatomical location, origin and insertion points, primary functions, biomechanical contributions, aesthetic significance, and relevant training or rehabilitation protocols.  
I am also integrating verified academic sources to ensure accuracy and accessibility of information.

I am evaluating publicly available datasets and digital repositories that offer detailed, accurate representations of human musculature.  
This includes assessing structural completeness, resolution quality, licensing compatibility, and integration potential with scientific workflows.  
Based on this evaluation, I will compile a structured JSON output reflecting the most viable and comprehensive anatomical resources.

I am designing a scalable JSON schema that interconnects muscles, tendons, nerves, joints, and exercises through unique identifiers.  
I am curating a substantial yet manageable sample dataset focusing on major anatomical entities relevant to exercise science.  
I am also identifying authoritative open-access resources where the full anatomical database can be programmatically retrieved.

I am systematically organizing foundational human anatomy data, focusing on major muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints relevant to fitness and movement science.  
I am verifying and compiling a curated list of authoritative, freely accessible scientific resources, including open-source 3D models, anatomical databases, and educational platforms, ensuring each is properly attributed and legally usable.  
My aim is to deliver a reliable, up-to-date, and ethically sourced reference that supports both learning and practical application in health and fitness domains.

I am synthesizing a curated collection of authoritative, openly accessible anatomical models and data, prioritizing scientific accuracy and usability.  
These include high-resolution 3D organ and musculoskeletal structures from trusted institutions like NIH, DBCLS, and Harvard-affiliated projects, all under permissive licenses.  
I am also integrating structured ontologies and practical tools to support research, education, and clinical applications across disciplines.

I am identifying reliable, openly licensed anatomical resources to ensure accuracy and compliance, prioritizing those with permissive licenses suitable for data extraction.  
I am organizing the information into a coherent schema that captures muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints with detailed attributes such as origin, insertion, function, and innervation.  
This structured approach enables the creation of a robust, reusable JSON dataset aligned with academic standards and open-access principles.

I am focusing on assembling a high-quality, curated subset of major muscles with detailed functional data, supported by reliable sources.  
I am leveraging open-access anatomical resources that provide structured data through standardized ontologies and downloadable models.  
These foundations enable scalable, accurate expansion of the dataset programmatically while ensuring scientific integrity.

Estoy consolidando fuentes confiables y abiertas, combinando la exhaustividad de Uberon y FMA con información funcional de OpenStax y Physiopedia, complementada con modelos 3D accesibles bajo licencias libres.  
El diseño del modelo se basa en identificadores únicos y relaciones claras entre estructuras anatómicas, asegurando interoperabilidad y rastreabilidad mediante referencias externas como FMA, Uberon y Wikidata.  
Finalmente, estoy estructurando los datos en formato JSON con un esquema coherente que facilita su uso en aplicaciones científicas, educativas o de simulación.

I am curating a meticulously structured overview of all major skeletal muscles, prioritizing accuracy and coverage while balancing practicality.  
I focus on delivering detailed profiles for the most essential muscles, supported by a compact taxonomy that includes all names and identifiers.  
The framework enables seamless expansion into full anatomical data through trusted external sources.

I am identifying reliable public resources, including anatomical databases and structured Wikipedia content, to ensure accuracy and completeness.  
I’m constructing a well-organized JSON structure that captures essential anatomical details—origin, insertion, function, associated exercises—while maintaining consistency across entries.  
The final deliverables include a core set of key muscles, a full index for reference, and dedicated tendon data, all designed for practical use in education and application development.

I am prioritizing clarity and conciseness by focusing on a curated set of representative muscle cards, reducing redundancy while preserving essential anatomical information.  
I aim to maintain comprehensive coverage through a streamlined index that captures key attributes for each structure without overwhelming the output.  
This approach ensures the response remains within practical limits while delivering meaningful, accessible insights.

I am synthesizing data from authoritative public repositories to compile accurate, standardized muscle anatomy entries.  
Each entry includes origin, insertion, and function, aligned with established anatomical nomenclature.  
The resulting dataset serves as a reliable seed for building a dynamic anatomical database.

I am constructing detailed descriptions of muscles, tendons, and nerves with accurate origins, insertions, functions, and innervations.  
I am ensuring clinical relevance by including pathologies and functional contexts such as epicondylitis or nerve entrapments.  
I am maintaining clarity and elegance while avoiding technical jargon overload or reference to tools or processes.

I am systematically organizing musculoskeletal anatomy into functional groups, aligning nerves, joints, and muscles with targeted rehab exercises and contraindicated movements.  
I ensure comprehensive coverage by integrating deep stabilizers like the pelvic floor, diaphragm, and intrinsic hand and foot muscles, while preserving the user’s original 18 groupings and filling in essential gaps.  
This structured approach enables precise, clinically relevant guidance tailored to both therapeutic intervention and risk mitigation.

I am mapping muscle groups to a regional taxonomy while preserving the user's existing categorizations and enriching them with precise anatomical relationships.  
I am verifying each term against authoritative sources to ensure accuracy and consistency with international standards.  
I am integrating structured data from reliable ontologies to enhance the depth and scientific validity of the classification.

I am identifying reliable, freely accessible sources for 3D models, anatomical nomenclature, and structured muscle data.  
My focus is on verifying licensing terms, especially CC-BY compliance, and locating machine-readable formats like JSON or CSV.  
I am compiling authoritative references that support accurate, reproducible anatomical mapping for research or educational use.

I am ensuring accuracy by avoiding speculative assignments of identifier values, recognizing the risks of introducing errors.  
Instead, I am relying on established ontologies and databases to validate relationships and attributes.  
The approach prioritizes integrity over immediacy, aligning with best practices in biomedical data curation.

I am cross-referencing anatomical terminology and identifiers to ensure accuracy, focusing on established databases like FMA and TA2.  
I consider the hierarchical relationships within anatomical classifications, particularly for skeletal muscles in humans.  
My goal is to provide reliable information by relying on trusted resources rather than assumptions.

I am identifying open-access, high-quality 3D muscle models suitable for medical, scientific, and academic use, prioritizing those with permissive licensing and direct downloadability.  
I evaluate each resource based on its availability, compliance with open science principles, and relevance to the user’s need for educational or research applications.  
My focus is on balancing accuracy, usability, and freedom from restrictive copyright barriers.

I am systematically evaluating publicly available anatomical datasets and visual materials to identify reliable, legally compliant sources for educational and research use.  
My focus includes 2D illustrations from Wikimedia Commons, such as public domain plates from Gray’s Anatomy and CC-BY-SA vector graphics, as well as structured data from Terminologia Anatomica and Wikidata.  
I am also verifying the availability of 3D models, including those from NIH’s 3D Print Exchange and BodyParts3D, ensuring their licensing permits reuse and redistribution.

tool_result.tool_observation:
The useful information in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_skeletal_muscles_of_the_human_body for user goal Confirm whether the muscle tables include identifier columns (FMA, TA98/TA2, Wikidata) and list the main muscle group sections covered as follows: Evidence in page: ## Table explanation and summary [edit] The muscles are described using anatomical terminology. The columns are as follows: | Name | Explanation | | --- | --- | | Muscle | US English[a] name of the muscle per Terminologia Anatomica (TA),[13] minus the term "muscle", with the words reordered occasionally for better sorting. Parts and bellies are listed out as separate rows, as they are sometimes considered separate muscles. - Anything denoting the muscles relationship to another muscle such as e.g. superior, inferior etc. should always be used as a suffix and not a prefix, to create better sortability of the list. | | Location | The location of the muscle in a standard human body. The location first specifies a group such as head, neck, torso, upper limbs, or lower limbs, then may have more specific information. However this additional information must be describing location not function. | | Origin | The bone or other structure the muscle is attached to that remains immobile during the action. The term "bone" is omitted from bone names. | | Insertion | The attachment point of the muscle, on a bone or otherwise, that moves during the action. | | Artery | The artery which supplies the muscle with blood. The term "artery" is included to avoid confusing columns. | | Nerve | The nerve(s) which tell the muscle to act (innervates the muscle). The term "nerve" is included for clarity. | | Action | The movement performed by the muscle from the standard anatomical position. In other positions, other actions may be performed. | | Antagonist | The muscle which can 'cancel' or to some degree reverse the action of the muscle. Muscle synergies are noted in parentheses when relevant. | | O (Occurrences) | Number of times that the named muscle row occurs in a standard human body. Here it may also be denoted when a given muscles only occurs in a male or a female body. By (F) for female and (M) for male, if nothing is denoted. The muscle can be assumed to occur in both genders. This gender denomination should always be behind the number, not in front of it. | | TA | The number of rows in the table for the relevant Terminologia Anatomica muscle. For example, TA splits the nasalis muscle into transverse and alar parts, so their TA column entries are 2. | ### Summary in numbers [edit] There does not appear to be a definitive source counting all skeletal muscles. Different sources group muscles differently, regarding physical features as different parts of a single muscle or as several muscles. Organizing anatomical knowledge with precision and purpose

I am consolidating authoritative anatomical identifiers from trusted sources, ensuring each property aligns with established scientific standards.  
The comprehensive muscle dataset from Wikipedia, enriched with standardized classifications and functional details, provides a robust foundation for accurate representation.  
I am now structuring this information into a coherent, reliable format that reflects both precision and completeness.

I am structuring the human musculoskeletal system by defining hierarchical muscle groups with precise identifiers, regional classifications, and comprehensive muscle listings in both Spanish and Latin. 2. **Origen/inserción/inervación/acción/antagonista**: scrapea la tabla de *List of skeletal muscles of the human body* (CC BY-SA), que ya trae esas columnas para ~289 filas/753 músculos [[extractor]]; complementa con OpenStax (CC BY 4.0) [[26]].
3. **Asset 3D por músculo**: usa el FMA ID obtenido para enlazar la pieza correspondiente en BodyParts3D [[14]] o buscarla en Z-Anatomy (CC BY-SA 4.0) [[5]].
4. **Ejercicios por músculo**: cruza tu BD de 1500 ejercicios contra el directorio músculo→ejercicio de ExRx [[79]].
5. **Rehab/lesiones**: enlaza artículos de Physiopedia (CC BY-SA) por entidad para los campos de rehab y riesgo [[89]].
6. **Imágenes 2D**: láminas de Gray's (dominio público) por nombre latino [[64]].

Ejemplo SPARQL (Wikidata, CC0) para el crosswalk:
```sparql
SELECT ?item ?lat ?fma ?ta2 WHERE {
  ?item wdt:P1402 ?fma.
  OPTIONAL { ?item wdt:P7173 ?ta2. }
  ?item rdfs:label ?lat. FILTER(LANG(?lat)="la")
} LIMIT 1000
```

Con esto tu app queda **100% trazable a estándares académicos** (TA2/FMA), con assets 3D/2D legales y relaciones músculo↔tendón↔nervio↔articulación↔ejercicio listas para consumir. ¿Quieres que en el siguiente paso genere las fichas detalladas del resto de músculos por lotes (p. ej., antebrazo + mano, o pierna completa)?

The useful information in https://docs.google.com/document/d/14DvWi5OtE8AToSQU0dFUIQCA11MlX0JIY01XEjVIldo/edit?usp=sharing for user goal Extract the audit findings, problems identified, and missing information mentioned in the document as follows: 

Evidence in page: 
## 1. RESUMEN EJECUTIVO DE LA AUDITORÍA

La arquitectura del proyecto que presentas es sólida y técnicamente acertada para una aplicación web moderna y de alto rendimiento. Elegir 2D SVG interactivo como capa base en combinación con Deep-linking / visores 3D (Z-Anatomy y BodyParts3D) resuelve de forma elegante los problemas de rendimiento en móviles, la falta de estandarización de nombres de malla en modelos 3D y las restricciones de licencias libres (CC BY-SA).

Sin embargo, tras analizar el código ejecutable y las bases de datos JSON, se identificaron omitidos clave en la cobertura anatómica, fallos de ejecución e inconsistencias en JavaScript/SVG y simplificaciones biomecánicas que comprometen la precisión científica requerida para una app de fitness y rehabilitación.

## 2. AUDITORÍA DE COBERTURA ANATÓMICA

### 2.1. Sistema Muscular (Evaluación de 147 Entidades / 27 Grupos)

- Estado Actual: El JSON 01_grupos_musculares.json lista 147 músculos/grupos clasificados en 27 categorías. No obstante, en 02_musculos_fichas.json solo existen 32 fichas detalladas (un 22% del total). El resto (115 músculos) recurren a un mensaje "stub-note" sin datos de origen, inserción o biomecánica.
- Agrupaciones Problemáticas para Fitness/Rehab:
    1. Cuádriceps (MUS-110): En las fichas se agrupó como una sola entidad. En entrenamiento y patología femoropatelar es crítico diferenciar el Vasto Medial Oblicuo (VMO) (alineación patelar), Vasto Lateral y Recto Femoral (único biarticular, no se estimula eficientemente en sentadillas debido a la Paradoja de Lombard).
    2. Isquiosurales (MUS-115): Agrupar Bíceps Femoral, Semitendinoso y Semimembranoso oculta que la Cabeza Corta del Bíceps Femoral es monoarticular (solo flexiona rodilla, no actúa en Peso Muerto Rumano/RDL) y que el desgarro en sprint ocurre predominantemente en la cabeza larga del bíceps femoral.
    3. Deltoides (MUS-063..065): Deben mantenerse como 3 haces independientes con diferentes planos de alineación de fibras respecto al plano escapular.
- Músculos Omisos Importantes:
    - Infraespinoso y Redondo Menor (manguito rotador posterior, imprescindibles en la desaceleración de lanzamientos y salud glenohumeral).
    - Poplíteo (el "desbloqueador" articular de la rodilla; clave en tendinitis poplítea).
    - Serrato Posterior Superior e Inferior (mecánica respiratoria y dolor torácico).
    - Tensor de la Fascia Lata (TFL) (síndrome de la centella o fricción de la banda iliotibial).
    - Coracobraquial (estabilidad anterior del hombro).
    - Pronador Cuadrado y Supinador Corto (estabilidad distal de antebrazo y codo).

### 2.2. Sistema Tendinoso (15 Tendones Registrados)

- Brechas Clínicas y de Entrenamiento:
    1. Falta de distinción entre Tendón Patelar y Tendón del Cuádriceps: Aunque ambos pertenecen al aparato extensor de la rodilla, la tendinopatía patelar ("rodilla del saltador") se trata con sentadilla declinada/Spanish squat, mientras que la del cuádriceps afecta la inserción superior de la rótula en levantadores pesados.
- Omisiones Fundamentales:
    - Tendón de la Pata de Ganso (Pes Anserinus): Inserción común de Semitendinoso, Grácil y Sartorio en tibia medial. Una de las bursitis/tendinitis más comunes en corredores.
    - Tendón del Psoas-Ilíaco: Causa principal del "resalte de cadera" (snapping hip syndrome).
    - Tendón Distal del Tríceps Braquial: Tendinopatía insertiva en olécranon muy común en press banca pesado y fondos.
    - Tendón del Pectoral Mayor (Inserción Humeral): Sitio crítico de desgarro en levantadores de potencia.
    - Tendones Abductor Largo y Extensor Corto del Pulgar: Responsables de la Tenosinovitis de De Quervain (frecuente por agarres y en CrossFit).

### 2.3. Sistema Nervioso (14 Nervios Registrados)

- Brechas Clínicas y Atrapamientos de Ejercicio:
    1. Nervio Interóseo Posterior (PIN - Ramo Profundo del Radial): Pasa por la arcada de Frohse en el supinador. Se confunde frecuentemente con codo de tenista (epicondilitis lateral) refractario a tratamiento.
    2. Nervio Obturador: Entrapamiento en el canal obturador, causa común de dolor inguinal crónico e inexplicable en atletas.
    3. Nervios Glúteos Superior e Inferior: Responsables de la inervación de glúteo medio y mayor; su inhibición o atrapamiento en el espacio subglúteo causa "amnesia glútea".
    4. Nervio Musculocutáneo: Inerva bíceps y braquial; vulnerable en tracciones violentas o hipertrofia del coracobraquial.
    5. Nervio Toracodorsal y Pectorales: Involucrados en el Síndrome del Desfiladero Torácico (TOS).

### 2.4. Sistema Articular (13 Articulaciones Registradas)

- Brechas Articulares:
    1. Articulación Esternoclavicular (SC): La única unión ósea real del miembro superior con el esqueleto axial. Fundamental para el ritmo escapulohumeral completo (>90° de elevación).
    2. Articulación Femoropatelar: Debe analizarse como entidad funcional separada de la femorotibial. El Síndrome de Dolor Femoropatelar (SDFP) es la consulta #1 por dolor de rodilla en gimnasios.
    3. Articulaciones Radioulnar Proximal y Distal (PRUJ / DRUJ): Gobiernan la pronosupinación del antebrazo; fallas aquí generan dolor en codo o muñeca durante culls con barra recta.
    4. Articulación Tibiofibular Superior: Causa de dolor lateral de rodilla en sentadilla profunda con rotación externa excesiva.

## 3. AUDITORÍA TÉCNICA Y ERRORES DE CÓDIGO DETECTADOS

During execution testing, the following technical bugs and integration issues were discovered:

| ID Bug | Componente | Error Detectado | Impacto | Solución Aplicada |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BUG-01 | renderFicha (JS) | Mapeo de propiedad inconsistente: el JSON usa e.musculo o e.mus, y algunos valores contienen rangos como "MUS-071..074". | Crasheaba el listener onclick o intentaba buscar el ID literal "MUS-071..074" en la BD, devolviendo undefined. | Se implementó un parser de rangos y unificación de propiedades (e.musculo || e.mus). |
| BUG-02 | SVG Highlight | Al seleccionar ejercicios como Curl de Bíceps (EX-06), el JS intenta iluminar MUS-067 (Braquial). Sin embargo, MUS-067 no existía como elemento <path> en el SVG. | Falla silenciosa: la interfaz listaba el músculo en texto pero el atlas no resaltaba ninguna zona visual. | Se dibujaron los trazados SVG para músculos profundos y se agregó lógica fallback para indicar la región si el SVG es omitido. |
| BUG-03 | viewOf Dictionary | El diccionario viewOf registraba la primera vista donde aparecía un ID. Si una articulación o nervio (ej. ART-001, NER-008) existía en ambas vistas, al buscarlo desde la vista posterior forzaba un cambio brusco a la vista anterior. | Mala UX en navegación y parpadeo de interfaz. | Se preserva la vista actual si la entidad está disponible en ambas ilustraciones SVG. |
| BUG-04 | Formato de Tooltip | El tooltip posicionado con e.clientX / e.clientY sufría desbordamiento (overflow) cerca de los bordes derecho e inferior de la pantalla en dispositivos con pantallas <1200px. | El texto del tooltip se cortaba fuera del viewport. | Se agregaron cláusulas de contención de bordes (Math.min con ancho de pantalla). |
| BUG-05 | Búsqueda por texto | La búsqueda no limpiaba los resaltados previos de ejercicios al hacer clic en un resultado de texto. | Confusión visual entre el ejercicio activo y el músculo individual seleccionado. | Se ejecuta clearSel() y reseteo de clases de ejercicio antes de renderizar la nueva selección. |

## 4. CORRECCIONES BIOMECÁNICAS Y APLICACIÓN AL ENTRENAMIENTO

Para elevar la calidad del atlas a un nivel académico y profesional de fitness, se han corregido los siguientes principios biomecánicos dentro del dataset de fichas:

1. Paradoja de Lombard y Selección de Ejercicios:
- Problema previo: Asignar la sentadilla como ejercicio estrella del cuádriceps sin especificar qué cabezas se estimulan.
- Corrección: La sentadilla genera contracción simultánea de cadera y rodilla; el Recto Femoral apenas cambia de longitud. Se indica explícitamente que para hipertrofiar/rehabilitar el Recto Femoral se requieren Extensiones de Rodilla o Sissy Squat, mientras que los Vastos dominan en la sentadilla.
2. Reclutamiento Diferencial de Isquiosurales:
- Problema previo: Asignar el Peso Muerto Rumano (RDL) para todo el grupo de isquiosurales.
- Corrección: El RDL estimula fuertemente las cabezas biarticulares (Semitendinoso, Semimembranoso, Bíceps Femoral Cabeza Larga). La Cabeza Corta del Bíceps Femoral únicamente se recluta en ejercicios de flexión de rodilla (Leg Curls).
3. Mecánica del Triceps Surae (Gastrocnemio vs. Sóleo):
- Problema previo: Elevación de talones genérica.
- Corrección: Con la rodilla extendida (de pie), el Gastrocnemio (biarticular) asume la mayor parte de la tensión. Con la rodilla flexionada a 90° (elevación de talón sentado), el Gastrocnemio se acorta activamente y el Sóleo asume más del 80% de la carga.

Summary: 
The audit identified several critical issues compromising the project's scientific accuracy and completeness. Key problems include significant gaps in anatomical coverage, where only 22% of muscles have detailed data, with the rest being placeholders. Major biomechanical simplifications were found, such as treating multi-part muscle groups (e.g., quadriceps, isquiosurales) as single entities, which is incorrect for training and rehab. The system also omits important structures like the popliteus muscle and key tendons like Pes Anserinus. Technically, there are bugs causing crashes and visual failures due to inconsistent property mapping and missing SVG paths for deep muscles. Furthermore, the document highlights a lack of distinction between clinically relevant but similar structures, such as the patellar and quadriceps tendons.

Identifying gaps and inconsistencies across anatomical systems and digital interface elements

I am addressing gaps in muscle detail by distinguishing individual components such as the VMO, vastus lateralis, and rectus femoris within the quadriceps, and separating the short head of the biceps femoris from the hamstrings due to its distinct biomechanics.  
I am integrating missing muscles including the infraspinatus, teres minor, popliteus, serratus posterior, TFL, coracobrachialis, pronator quadratus, and supinator to ensure full anatomical coverage.  
Additionally, I am adding the previously omitted tendons—Pes Anserinus and Psoas-Iliacus—as well as their distal connections to complete the structural integrity of the system.

I am assessing structural omissions in musculoskeletal and nervous system components, noting absent tendons, nerves, and joints that compromise anatomical completeness  
Simultaneously, I am evaluating technical flaws affecting data consistency, visual rendering, and user interaction, particularly around property mapping, hidden muscle visibility, and responsive design challenges  
These observations guide a holistic refinement of both content accuracy and interactive functionality to ensure seamless, precise anatomical representation
